newsitem.title: USA: US wants open financial markets after Thai crisis.
newsitem.headline: US wants open financial markets after Thai crisis.

text.p: A U.S. Treasury official, lobbying for open financial markets as the next stage of trade reform, said on Tuesday that the Thai crisis should not be allowed to reverse the drive to freer global banking rules.

Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers told a congressional group that the United States was ready for some compromises to ensure a financial services package went ahead at the World Trade Organisation, which fights for freer trade.
But Washington would not sign a deal which did not meet U.S. interests just for the sake of meeting a deadline.
"If the agreement on the table is not good enough, we will not sign it," Summers said. "We will not take it unless and until sufficient offers are forthcoming from other countries."

Developing countries, including some in Southeast Asia, have been the main critics of plans to ease trade rules in financial services, arguing that giving foreign firms access to their markets could hurt domestic banks or threaten security by boosting access to fickle speculative capital.
Some say Thailand's relatively open markets simply encouraged speculation, triggering a currency crunch which tore Thailand's reputation as a booming Tiger economy to shreds.
But Summers said Thailand's "unsustainable macroeconomic policy mix" was the main factor behind the financial problems.

"Relatively open capital markets, independent monetary policies and a current account deficit of eight percent of gross domestic product do not mix," he said. "The speculative activity we saw in the weeks leading to the crisis was the result, not the cause, of Thailand's problems."
Thailand won $16 billion in loans from the International Monetary Fund and neighbour states on Monday and promised to adopt a package of IMF-backed reforms.
Summers said measures to improve the health and transparency of the Thai banking system would form a substantial element of the IMF package, which the United States expected to be able to support.
The United States has already promised to back a WTO financial services pact by offering "substantially full market access" to foreign firms in the domestic financial sector.
Leading industrialised countries said in June that they hoped a deal could be in place by the end of this year.
"Liberalization in the financial services sector is the next and perhaps the final frontier in worldwide efforts to move to more open markets," Summers said.
"We believe the whole world stands to gain from a global, efficient capital market."
He said problems in Southeast Asia had increased the U.S. will to strengthen financial systems and make them more open.
"We believe these to be complementary not conflicting goals and we will go the extra mile to convince doubtful emerging economies this is the case," he said.
